Calico vs Cascadia: Which Tile-Laying Puzzle Fits Your Table

2026-10-30

Calico vs Cascadia comes down to one question. Do you want a tile puzzle that forgives a bad placement, or one that charges you for it until the last turn?

If you want the answer with no scrolling, here it is. Buy Cascadia if you have never played a tile-laying game. It runs about $37, teaches in 10 minutes, and shows you every option before you commit. Buy Calico if you already love this kind of spatial puzzle and want one that squeezes harder. It runs about $42.

Both come from Flatout Games and both were illustrated by Beth Sobel, so the spec sheet cannot separate them. Both play 1 to 4 players in 30 to 45 minutes. I own both, and Cascadia has hit my table more than 40 times against about 12 for Calico. That gap is not about which game is better, and it is the thing most comparisons skip.

What a Tile Puzzle Actually Asks of You

Here is the key insight. Every tile-laying game is two games stacked on top of each other. One is the spatial puzzle in front of you. The other is the draft, the shared market you pull tiles from. Games feel tight or loose depending on which of those two you can control, and Calico and Cascadia hand you very different amounts of control over both.

Start with the puzzle. In Calico you hold two patch tiles in hand and place one into an empty space on your quilt board. Each patch has a color and a pattern. Colors earn buttons, patterns attract cats, and three Design Goal tiles along the border check the six patches around them at the end of the game. Every placement is permanent. There is no rearranging, ever.

In Cascadia you take one of four face-up pairs, a habitat tile and a wildlife token, and add the tile to your landscape. Matching terrain is not required to place a tile. It only matters when corridors score at the end. Then you drop the wildlife token onto any empty tile showing that species, which can be a tile you placed five turns ago.

That one rule is the whole personality of the game. The worst habitat tile in the Cascadia box can still be buried somewhere cheap. The worst patch in Calico has to live in your quilt until the game ends.

Now the draft. Cascadia shows four pairs at all times. Nothing is hidden, and a Nature Token can even let you split a pair and take the tile and animal you actually want. Calico shows you three patch tiles in the market, and when you take one, the refill comes blind from the bag. You can see your next two options, and after that you are guessing with everyone else.

But here is where the two games split again. The market is where both get their interaction. Somebody takes the pair you needed, and now three turns of planning are dead. Notice that neither game lets you touch another player's board. Cascadia's ending and Calico's ending are both personal, quiet, and a little lonely. The fight happens over tiles, not over territory.

Two Numbers That Decide It For You

Pay attention to this number: zero. That is how many empty spaces you have left at the end of Calico. Your quilt fills completely, so the last few turns are not about scoring anything new. They are about fitting whatever is left into the gap you saved. When I finish a Calico game I feel like I solved something. Whether I solved it well is a separate question.

The Cascadia number is 20. You take exactly 20 turns in the base game, then the habitat tiles run out. Your map is never finished. It just stops. My first five games of Cascadia all ended with mountains I never connected and a salmon card I ignored completely.

Here is why that matters at your table. Materials that run out create a rush, and boards that fill up create dread. If your group plays slow, Cascadia's clock keeps things moving because everyone gets the same 20 turns. If your group likes the satisfaction of a completed build, Calico gives you that finished quilt to look at afterward.

The Difference Nobody Mentions

I thought I understood both games after a year of playing them. Then I did the boring thing and wrote down my scores.

Here is the contradiction. Every ranking calls Cascadia the lighter game, and lighter usually means less to think about. My log says the opposite. On my last ten plays of Calico I never felt out of the game until the final third, because I still had spaces left to fill. On three of those ten plays of Cascadia I lost the game in the draft around turn 6, watching a pair I needed go to someone else twice in a row before the first round was over. The lighter game is the one that punished my drafting earlier.

However, the reason comes down to market size. Cascadia hands you four visible pairs and 20 turns, which means the draft is a real fight you can lose. Calico hides the refill, so early on you cannot punish anyone on purpose. You just take the best of three and hope the bag is kind.

That is the whole twist. Cascadia is not a soft game with easy decisions. It is a soft game with sharp decisions, and it puts them in the first ten minutes. Calico spreads its pressure across the whole board, and its bite comes later, when you realize the pattern you committed to in turn 4 cannot be finished.

When Calico Wins

Calico is a quilt puzzle from designer Kevin Russ, published in 2020 by Flatout Games and AEG. You are competing to sew the coziest quilt. Same-color groups earn you buttons, defined pattern groups attract cats, and the three Design Goal tiles on your board want specific groupings of colors and patterns around them. It won the 2020 American Tabletop Award for Game of the Year, and the art is the reason half the people who own it bought it.

Where it wins is at the moment a plan lands. In my best game I chained a triple of teal patches into a button while the same three patches completed a cat pattern, and the Design Goal next to them paid out too. Four scoring systems, one placement. Cascadia rarely gives you that, because its wildlife cards only ever ask one question at a time.

Calico is also the better solo game of the two if you like a strict puzzle. The goal is a score, not a finish line, and my best is 61. The honest flaw, and the reason mine only comes out a few times a year, is that a badly tangled quilt is painful to finish. When I took the wrong pattern in turn 5 of a recent game, I still had 20 minutes of placing tiles with nothing left to win. Calico has no mercy mechanic. The board does not care that you are stuck.

When Cascadia Wins

Cascadia is a habitat-building game from designer Randy Flynn, published by Flatout Games in 2021. You draft pairs, grow a Pacific Northwest landscape, and score two ways. Habitat corridors reward the largest connected group of each terrain. Wildlife tokens score against whichever cards are active that game, so the hawk wants your birds lined up one way and the bear wants family groups another.

It won the 2022 Spiel des Jahres, the biggest award in board games, and the 2023 International Gamers Award for best solo game. My wife has never asked to play a board game twice in one night except this one.

Where it wins is teaching. I have taught Cascadia to six people who had never played a modern board game, and every single one was making real choices by turn 3. The family variant drops the math for younger kids, and the box comes with enough scoring cards that the puzzle changes between plays.

The honest flaw is the criticism the award reviews all level at it: there is almost no interaction. Nobody attacks you. Two players can sit at the same table, build their own landscapes, and compare scores at the end. If your group needs banter or table talk in a game, Cascadia will feel like four people doing homework next to each other. My group plays it on quiet weeknights and saves the loud games for the weekend.

If you need five or six players, the Cascadia: Landmarks expansion adds a fifth and sixth player along with new scenario cards. It was about $33 when I checked, which is close to what the base game costs, so only buy it if your table is actually that big.

The Third Option: Knitting Circle

If the Calico puzzle sounds good but the $42 and the mercy-free scoring do not, look at Knitting Circle. It is a standalone follow-up to Calico from the same studio. You are a knitter laying yarn tiles into patterns instead of a quilter laying patches, and it plays 1 to 4 in the same 30 to 45 minute window.

It costs $31, which is the cheapest of the three, and it is the easiest to teach to a mixed table. If you already own Calico and want a second box with the same feel for a different group, this is the one I would grab before any expansion.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would this box survive 10 plays on a shelf that already holds 40 games? Plenty of tile puzzles do not. They get one evening of wonder and then become decoration.

Cascadia passes on replay value alone. The wildlife scoring cards rotate, the scenarios change the goals, and it plays at every player count without falling apart. I am at 40 plays and still seeing setups I have not tried.

Calico passes for a smaller reason. It survives because of the score. Each game is a number, and a number you can beat is a game you come back to. It is the only game in my collection where a friend texted me a screenshot of a 74 two days after learning it.

Ten plays is the bar. If only one of these makes it there in your house, I would bet on the one you can teach to a stranger without a rulebook open. That is Cascadia in most homes.

Here is the part that matters. For a first tile-laying game, grab Cascadia at about $37. If you already know the genre and want the tighter puzzle, grab Calico at about $42. Prices bounce, so catch Cascadia under $35 and Calico under $40 and you have done well.
